summary: Choosing a suitable lunar South Pole landing site is challenging because sunlight, terrain conditions, and communication opportunities with Earth vary between locations and over time. Existing tools, such as NASA Moon Trek, can be complex for beginners and the public. To address this problem, we developed the Lunar South Pole Landing Simulator, an interactive web application that allows users to compare CLPS landing sites and Artemis candidate regions. It provides dynamic 2D visualizations of the Sun's and Earth's positions, illumination and slope information, communication risk indicators, and Sunset and Earthset warnings. It also includes an AI Copilot for mission suggestions and a beginner-friendly tutorial. Built with HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript, and Canvas, the application integrates Groq API (Llama 3) through Cloudflare Workers. Despite having no previous programming experience, our team successfully developed this prototype. We learned about NASA datasets, API integration, and teamwork. In the future, we plan to integrate JPL Horizons API and higher-resolution LOLA terrain data to improve scientific accuracy.
details:
Lunar South Pole Landing Simulator

Project Overview
The Lunar South Pole Landing Simulator is an interactive web application designed to evaluate potential human landing missions on the Moon. The lunar South Pole presents extreme environmental challenges, including prolonged periods of darkness and complete communication blackouts due to the lack of direct line-of-sight to Earth. The simulator bridges the gap between complex aerospace datasets and public understanding by combining real-world NASA telemetry with a 2D visual interface and an integrated Artificial Intelligence assistant. It allows mission planners, educators, and the general public to rapidly compare landing sites, assess solar power potential, and evaluate communication windows.

Detailed Features

First, Mission Briefing and Onboarding. Upon opening the application, users are presented with a welcome briefing modal. This screen establishes the historical and scientific context of returning to the Moon. It explains that the South Pole contains permanently shadowed craters with water ice, a critical resource for producing drinking water, oxygen, and rocket fuel. The briefing outlines three critical telemetry parameters that dictate mission success. It explains that illumination is vital because a lunar day lasts 29.5 Earth days and low sun angles cause long shadows. It notes that terrain slope exceeding ten degrees poses a risk of tipping the lander over. Finally, it clarifies that an Earthset results in a complete loss of direct communication. This onboarding ensures users understand the fundamental physics before interacting with the simulation.

Second, Interactive 2D Telemetry Viewport. The primary visual component is an HTML5 Canvas that dynamically renders a 2D representation of the lunar surface and the starry sky. The system calculates the Sun's elevation angle based on the user's selected simulation date and time. As the user adjusts the timeline, the sun visually moves across the sky. This movement directly corresponds to the calculated solar illumination percentage displayed on the screen, providing an immediate and intuitive understanding of how solar power availability changes over time at the selected location.

Third, Comprehensive Landing Site Database. The control panel includes a curated dropdown menu featuring fourteen distinct landing sites, categorized by their mission objectives. It includes current Artemis III candidates such as Peak near Cabeus B, Haworth, and Malapert Massif. It includes historical and international sites such as Apollo 11, Apollo 17, and Chandrayaan-3. It also includes commercial targets such as Malapert A and Nobile Crater. This allows users to compare historical equatorial sites with future polar missions. Additionally, users can adjust the simulation date, time, and crew size, which is restricted to a range of two to four astronauts.

Fourth, Dynamic Risk Assessment and Warning System. Based on the selected site and the calculated solar conditions, the right-side telemetry panel updates in real-time. It displays exact coordinates, terrain slope, calculated illumination percentage, and the baseline risk level for that specific site. The system includes an automated warning mechanism. If the calculated illumination falls below sixty percent, a prominent red warning box automatically appears in the telemetry panel. This alerts the user to the extreme risk of a sunset event, which would result in a total loss of solar power generation.

Fifth, AI Mission Analysis and Evaluation. The application features a distinct Save and Analyze Mission button. When clicked, the system utilizes hard-coded physics logic to determine if the current mission configuration is safe, based on illumination thresholds and slope inclines. Following this determination, a Large Language Model generates a professional, concise flight director report. If conditions are safe, the interface displays a green Mission Success panel. If conditions are unsafe, it displays a red Mission Failed panel, accompanied by an AI-generated sentence explaining the specific failure point, such as insufficient solar power or dangerous terrain.

Sixth, Floating AI Copilot and Security Protocol. Located in the bottom right corner of the interface is a persistent floating robot icon. Clicking this icon opens an interactive chat window. Users can ask natural language questions about the current simulation data. The AI Copilot utilizes the active telemetry data as context to provide accurate answers. Importantly, the system is equipped with a robust security protocol. The AI is instructed to analyze user input for inappropriate language or profanity. If detected, it immediately halts the response and displays a standardized security warning, ensuring the application remains a safe and professional educational tool.

Seventh, Navigation and Mission Dashboard. The application features a clean, responsive top navigation bar. On the top left, a Tutorial button allows users to easily review the mission guidelines at any time. On the top right, an Information button opens a comprehensive Mission Dashboard. This dashboard contains a grid of direct external links to official NASA and JPL resources, including the Artemis III mission page, the CLPS program, the VIPER rover, and the JPL Horizons system. This encourages users to explore real-world data beyond the simulation.

Eighth, Immersive Audio-Visual Experience. The application utilizes a custom deep-space user interface featuring glassmorphism effects, utilizing semi-transparent backgrounds with backdrop blurring. The background music track was entirely composed and produced from scratch by the team using MuseScore Studio 4, providing an original and immersive mission-control soundtrack. A toggle button is provided in the bottom left corner to activate or mute this custom audio. The layout is strictly responsive, ensuring all telemetry data and controls remain accessible across different screen sizes.

Technical Implementation

The frontend is built entirely using standard web technologies including HTML5, CSS3, and Vanilla JavaScript, with the HTML5 Canvas API handling the 2D visualizations. The AI functionality is powered by a Large Language Model through the Groq API. To ensure security and bypass browser Cross-Origin Resource Sharing restrictions, all AI requests are securely routed through a serverless Cloudflare Worker proxy. The telemetry data and site coordinates utilized in the database were derived from official NASA Technical Reports Server documents, Artemis III landing site updates, and Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera datasets.
